newsitem.title: JAPAN: NTT gearing up for multimedia network service.
newsitem.headline: NTT gearing up for multimedia network service.

text.p: Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp, aiming to transform itself from a phone firm into a multimedia superpower, will launch a new network business in January to tap explosive demand for computer communications.

The telecoms goliath also plans to open up its network for use by rival Internet access providers and leased-line providers, partly to counter support for the government's proposed break-up of the company.
The new service, called the Open Computer Network (OCN), will be a data transmission network giving users access to the Internet and private lines for computer communications.
The network will provide a platform for NTT to move into new areas, such as software and cross-border services. Japanese law currently limits NTT's operations to domestic services.

The system will use routers, which cost only a small fraction of conventional telephone exchange systems used in voice communications. NTT will spend only 12 billion yen ($110 million) on the project during its first year.

"The OCN service is the mainstay of our next-generation multimedia business," said Masamichi Tanabe, NTT's senior vice president in charge of multimedia services. "Inquiries (about the OCN) are flooding in. We need to respond to our customers' demands for low-cost international network services."
He said NTT hopes eventually, through affiliates, to launch businesses such as security-related applications on the OCN.
The new network will also pose a serious threat to existing Internet and leased-line providers that use more expensive systems such as telephone exchanges.

NTT will charge 30,000 yen ($275) to 40,000 yen ($366) a month for a 128 kbps (kilobits per second) OCN line. Leased lines of that speed using telephone exchange systems cost 280,000 yen ($2,568) a month for Osaka-Tokyo services.
Though five times as fast as a conventional phone line, 128 kbps is a comparatively low speed for computer communications.
"We are concerned. There are a lot of customers who would prefer such a cheap service (as OCN) even if it's of lesser quality," said a spokesman at Japan Telecom Co, an NTT rival.
"Considering its brand image and the strength in the local call market, NTT will be able to acquire half Japan's Internet access service market," said Goldman Sachs analyst Eric Gan.

According to industry estimates, Japan's Internet access service market totaled 25 billion yen ($229 million) in 1995, and will balloon to between 200 billion yen ($1.83 billion) and 300 billion yen ($2.75 billion) in 2000.
Moreover, the OCN service is expected to strengthen NTT's earnings structure by boosting profits from local calls and sales of high-speed digital connections.

Gan expects profits from local calls to catch up with those from long-distance calls within two years, buoyed by users utilising the OCN to access the Internet and other communications services through their personal computers.
Long-distance services now account for roughly 75 percent of NTT's parent operating profits, Gan said.
A more important concern for NTT, however, is the pending government decision, expected during a parliament session due to begin next February, on whether to split up the company.

Officials at NTT are eager to give the impression that they will cooperate with other firms and allow open access to the OCN, and to avoid stirring up fears that they are trying to gain monopolistic advantage in information services. Such fears would refuel the calls for an NTT break-up.
Tanabe says competing firms will be able to use OCN's local loops at low rates to launch their own services. "We have no intention of becoming the sole winner in this OCN business."
But some industry officials are sceptical, saying NTT may forget this open philosophy once the break-up debate ends.
"NTT will have to go slowly, at least in the beginning, so as not to take away too much revenue from existing operators," said Kiyohisa Ota, an analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc. ($1=109 yen)
